questions.q: Why is `latest` a risky tag to rely on for reproducibility, per this lesson?
options: It's reserved and cannot actually be pushed to
It only works with private repositories
It's an ordinary, overwritable tag — just whatever was last pushed without an explicit version
It always points to the oldest version of an image
questions.explain: `latest` isn't a special guarantee — it's an ordinary tag that gets reassigned to whatever is pushed next without an explicit version.

questions.q: Why does a virtual machine typically take a minute or more to start, versus about a second for a comparable container?
options: Virtual machines are always run on remote, higher-latency servers
Virtual machines use slower storage hardware
A VM boots an entire guest operating system and kernel on a hypervisor, which a container skips
Containers are always smaller files than virtual machine disk images
questions.explain: The VM has to boot a full guest OS and kernel; a container just starts an isolated process on the kernel that's already running.

questions.q: In the example compose.yaml, what's the difference between the `api` and `redis` services?
options: api pulls a published image; redis builds from a Dockerfile
There is no difference — both behave identically
api builds from a local Dockerfile; redis pulls a published image
redis requires a separate docker run command; api does not
questions.explain: `build: .` builds from the local Dockerfile, while `image: redis:7-alpine` pulls an already-published image — the two ways a service can get its container.

questions.q: What does the EXPOSE instruction actually do?
options: It opens the specified port so traffic can reach the container
It documents which port the app expects — it does not open the port itself
It installs a web server inside the image
It removes a port from the container's network interface
questions.explain: EXPOSE is documentation. Actually publishing a port to the host happens with the -p flag at `docker run`, covered in Lesson 4.

questions.q: Why does the dependency-layer caching pattern from Lesson 3 matter even more for an AI app's Dockerfile?
options: AI apps never need a requirements.txt file
Packages like torch or transformers are much larger than typical web dependencies, so an uncached reinstall costs minutes, not seconds
AI apps cannot use a base image smaller than 1GB
Caching only works for Flask applications
questions.explain: A full dependency reinstall for a PyTorch-style stack is far more expensive than for a typical web framework, so avoiding unnecessary cache invalidation matters more.

questions.q: Why doesn't a container get GPU access by default, even on a machine that has a GPU?
options: A container's isolation hides host hardware like the GPU by default; it needs an explicit path to the driver
GPUs cannot be used by any containerized process
Only Windows containers support GPU access
Docker Desktop disables GPU access permanently
questions.explain: The same isolation that makes containers lightweight also hides host hardware like a GPU unless something explicitly passes it through.

questions.q: What's the key difference between a Dockerfile's `ENV` and `docker run`'s `-e` flag?
options: ENV is baked into the image at build time, visible to anyone who pulls it; -e is supplied only when a container starts
There is no difference — they behave identically
-e can only be used for numeric values
ENV only works with Python images
questions.explain: ENV becomes part of the image itself; -e exists only for that one running container and is never written to the image.

questions.q: What's the main downside of baking a large model checkpoint directly into an image with COPY?
options: It makes every build, push, and pull slower, and the registry stores a multi-gigabyte blob per image version
COPY cannot be used with files larger than 1MB
It requires a GPU to build
It automatically deletes the application code
questions.explain: Baked-in weights bloat the image, slowing the build/push/pull cycle and duplicating large blobs across image versions even when only the code changed.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say gateway-level rate limiting matters more for an AI app than a typical CRUD API?
options: AI apps never need authentication, so rate limiting is the only protection available
AI inference calls are comparatively slow and expensive, so a careless client loop can run up a large bill or cause an outage fast
CRUD APIs cannot be deployed behind a gateway at all
AI apps don't use HTTPS, so gateways handle encryption instead
questions.explain: A plain CRUD API's requests are small and cheap; an AI app's prompt payloads and inference calls are larger and far more expensive per request, so unmetered traffic is a bigger risk.

questions.q: What does a service's 'default domain' refer to, in this lesson's deploy walkthrough?
options: The real, public HTTPS URL the platform assigns once the service is running
The internal-only hostname used for container-to-container traffic
The name of the Dockerfile used to build the image
A placeholder URL that must be manually replaced before going live
questions.explain: Once the service reaches 'Running,' the console shows a default domain: a real public URL someone else can call.

questions.q: What actually happens at the moment of a blue-green cutover, per this lesson?
options: A full redeploy of the application to new servers
A routing change at the gateway/load balancer, not a redeploy
Both environments are torn down and rebuilt simultaneously
The model weights are retrained on the new instance
questions.explain: The cutover is just a routing switch -- that's exactly what makes it near-instant in either direction.

questions.q: Why can a rolling update briefly serve two different, both 'correct,' answers to the same question?
options: Because the load balancer is broken during a rollout
Because old and new instances run different, unrelated application code
Because old and new versions serve traffic at the same time, and can be running different model checkpoints
Because rolling updates always disable the model entirely during rollout
questions.explain: The side-by-side window means a request can land on an old-checkpoint instance or a new-checkpoint instance at the same moment, mid-rollout.

questions.q: According to this lesson, why do spot instances fit a queue-and-worker architecture better than a synchronous request a user is actively waiting on?
options: Spot instances are not compatible with queues at all
A reclaimed worker just means the job gets retried by another worker, rather than a user seeing an error
Queue-and-worker architectures never use GPUs
Synchronous requests are always cheaper than async ones
questions.explain: A queued job tolerates losing a worker mid-task because another worker can simply retry it -- a live, waiting user cannot tolerate that the same way.

questions.q: How does semantic caching decide whether a new prompt can reuse a cached response?
options: It requires the new prompt's text to match a stored prompt character-for-character
It compares the new prompt's embedding against stored prompts' embeddings for similarity
It always reuses the most recently cached response regardless of content
It checks whether the user's account ID matches a cached user
questions.explain: Semantic caching embeds the new prompt and compares it to stored prompt embeddings -- similar enough, and the cached response is reused.

questions.q: What does the 'max instances' setting protect against?
options: Cold starts during low-traffic periods
Model checkpoint mismatches between instances
Your budget and GPU quota from a runaway traffic spike or a bug
Slow image builds during CI/CD
questions.explain: Max instances caps scaling so a traffic spike or bug doesn't translate into an unconstrained bill or exceed a GPU quota.

questions.q: In the asynchronous pattern described in this lesson, what does the client receive immediately after submitting a request?
options: The final generated response
A job ID, with the result fetched or pushed later
A permanent error message
A new container image
questions.explain: Async returns a job ID right away; the client polls or receives a webhook for the actual result once a worker finishes it.

questions.q: What does deploying FeedbackScope in this lesson reuse from Lesson 12?
options: A requirement to use AWS App Runner specifically, with no alternative
The same rollback mechanism used for rolling updates
The exact same container image, unmodified
The two-screen pattern: point the platform at the image and port, then add a health check
questions.explain: This capstone deploy step is explicitly the same build-config / service-config pattern taught in Lesson 12.

questions.q: By the end of this capstone, what is FeedbackScope, per this lesson?
options: An untested prototype that never actually ran
A manually-scaled service with no autoscaling policy
A containerized, deployed, and autoscaled service where every configuration choice has a stated reason
A service that still runs on the developer's laptop only
questions.explain: That's the lesson's own summary of what the two prior lessons actually produced -- not just a running service, but one with justified configuration.

questions.q: According to this lesson's structure, what gets built in Lesson 24?
options: The initial Dockerfile and first deploy
A real autoscaling policy, a health check endpoint, and a caching decision
The final portfolio presentation
A completely new, unrelated project
questions.explain: Lesson 24 is 'Adding Autoscaling' -- it adds the autoscaling policy, health check, and caching decision on top of the already-deployed service.

questions.q: Why is max_instances capped at 5 in this capstone's policy?
options: As a hard ceiling on cost, since this is a portfolio project without a production budget
Because 5 is the maximum any cloud provider allows
Because higher counts would exceed the model's accuracy limits
Because the health check only supports 5 concurrent instances
questions.explain: Max instances here is explicitly a cost ceiling appropriate for a learning project's real but small cloud bill.
